'''Reinhard Oehme''' ({{IPA|de|ˈøːmə|lang}}; born 26 January 1928, [[Wiesbaden]]; died sometime between 29 September and 4 October 2010, [[Hyde Park, Chicago|Hyde Park]]<ref name="Obit-UoC">{{cite web |url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/reinhard-oehme-theoretical-physicist-1928-2010 |title=Reinhard Oehme, theoretical physicist, 1928–2010 |work=University of Chicago |date=2010-10-12 |access-date=2018-11-04}}</ref>) was a [[German-American]] [[physicist]] known for the discovery of C ([[C-symmetry|charge conjugation]]) non-conservation in the presence of P ([[parity (physics)|parity]]) violation, the formulation and proof of [[hadron]] [[dispersion relations]], the [[edge-of-the-wedge theorem]] in the function theory of several complex variables, the Goldberger–Miyazawa–Oehme [[sum rule in quantum mechanics|sum rule]], reduction of [[quantum field theories]], Oehme–Zimmermann [[superconvergence]] relations for [[gauge theory|gauge field]] [[correlation functions]], and many other contributions.

Oehme was born in Wiesbaden, Germany as the son of  Dr. Reinhold Oehme and Katharina Kraus. In 1952, in [[São Paulo]], Brazil, he married Mafalda Pisani, who was born in Berlin as the daughter of Giacopo Pisani and Wanda d'Alfonso. Mafalda died in Chicago in August of the year 2004.

==Education and career==

Completing the ''Abitur'' at the Rheingau Gymnasium in [[Geisenheim]] near Wiesbaden, Oehme started to study physics and mathematics at the [[Goethe University Frankfurt]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://inspirehep.net/author/profile/R.Oehme.1|title = Inspire}}</ref> receiving the Diploma in 1948 as student of [[Erwin Madelung]].<ref>HTML {{cite web |url=http://www.uni-frankfurt.de/fb/fb13/Dateien/paf/paf73.html |title=Erwin Madelung - Goethe-Universität |accessdate=2012-05-08 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212130742/http://www.uni-frankfurt.de/fb/fb13/Dateien/paf/paf73.html |archivedate=2012-02-12 }} See third last paragraph; translation of relevant passage: “As [[Friedrich Hund]] found out, directly after the war MADELUNG had particularly capable students and collaborators. Here we mention the following physicists, whose later successful career became known: ..., REINHARD OEHME (Professor of Theoretical Physics, Chicago) ....”</ref>
Then he moved to [[Göttingen]], joining the [[Max Planck Institute for Physics]] as a doctoral student of  [[Werner Heisenberg]], who was also a professor at the [[University of Göttingen]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://inspirehep.net/author/profile/W.Heisenberg.1|title=Inspire}}</ref><ref>[[Peter Freund]] (2007). ''A Passion for Discovery'', p.13. World Scientific Pub. Co., London. {{ISBN|981-270-646-1}}.</ref> Early in 1951, Oehme completed the requirements for his Dr.rer.nat. at the University of Göttingen. The translation of the title of his thesis is: "Creation of [[Photon]]s in Collisions of [[Nucleon]]s”<ref>Reinhard Oehme, [http://www.springerlink.com/content/g17ml6546537081x/?p=ec3ff738bf0d47a6b0af26c1c40a7941&pi=9,  Z. Physik 129, 573 (1951)]{{dead link|date=February 2020|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}},
“Erzeugung von Photonen beim Zusammenstoß von Nukleonen“. Eingegangen: 28. Februar 1951. (See end of Abstract for the appreciation of his teacher Werner Heisenberg).</ref> Later this year, Heisenberg asked him to join [[Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker]] on a trip to Brazil for the start-up of the Instituto de Física Teórica in São Paulo,<ref>http://www.ift.unesp.br/ (See Instituição, HISTÓRICO, third paragraph)</ref> considered also as a possible escape in view of the tense situation in Europe. In 1953, he returned to his assistant position at the Max Planck Institute in Göttingen. During the early fifties, the institute was a most interesting place. Oehme was there among an exceptional group of people around Heisenberg, including [[Vladimir Glaser]], [[Rolf Hagedorn]], [[Fritz Houtermans]], [[Gerhart Lüders]], [[Walter Thirring]], [[Kurt Symanzik]], [[Carl Friedrich von Weizsaecker]], [[Wolfhart Zimmermann]], [[Bruno Zumino]], who all have made important contributions to physics at some time. A year later, with Heisenberg's recommendation to his friend [[Enrico Fermi]], Oehme was offered a research associate position at the [[University of Chicago]], where he worked at the [[Institute for Nuclear Studies]]. Publications associated with this period are described below under Work. In the fall of 1956, he moved to Princeton as a member of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://library.ias.edu/hs/da/cos.pdf |title=Archived copy |accessdate=2008-07-26 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100609103054/http://library.ias.edu/hs/da/cos.pdf |archivedate=2010-06-09 }} (See page 297)</ref> returning in 1958 to the University of Chicago as a professor in the department of physics and at the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] for Nuclear Studies. In 1998, he became professor emeritus.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://physics.uchicago.edu/research/areas/particle_t.html#Oehme |title=Faculty, Physics Department: Reinhard Oehme |work=University of Chicago |date=February 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081009225941/http://physics.uchicago.edu/research/areas/particle_t.html#Oehme |archive-date=2008-10-09}}</ref>

=== Awards{{efn|name=citations}} ===
[[Guggenheim Fellow]], 1963–64;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/reinhard-oehme/ |title=Reinhard Oehme |work=Guggenheim Fellows |access-date=2018-11-04}} with photo</ref> [[Humboldt Price]], 1974; Fellowship of the Japanese Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) 1976, 1988.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://physics.uchicago.edu:80/about/honors/index.html |ref=Oehme |title=Honors by Faculty, U of Chicago |date=October 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081011061349/http://physics.uchicago.edu/about/honors/index.html |archive-date=2008-10-11 |access-date=2020-02-13 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The [[University of Chicago]] offers annually the ''Enrico Fermi, Robert R. McCormick & Mafalda and Reinhard Oehme Postdoctoral Research Fellowships''.<ref>{{cite web|title=Postdoctoral Fellowships|url=https://efi.uchicago.edu/fellowships|accessdate=2018-11-04}}</ref>

==Work==

===Dispersion relations, GMO sum rule, and edge-of-the-wedge theorem===

In 1954 in Chicago, Oehme studied the analytic properties of forward [[scattering amplitude]]s in [[quantum field theories]].{{Clarify|date=October 2025}} He found that particle-particle and [[antiparticle]]-particle amplitudes are connected by [[analytic continuation]] in the complex energy plane. These results led to the paper by him with [[Marvin L. Goldberger]]
and [[Hironari Miyazawa]] on the [[dispersion relations]] for [[pion]]-[[nucleon]] scattering, which also contains the Goldberger–Miyazawa–Oehme sum rule.
<ref>M. L. Goldberger, H. Miyazawa, and R. Oehme  [https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.99.986 , Phys. Rev. 99, 986 - 988 (1955)]
"Application of Dispersion Relations to [[Pion]]-Nucleon Scattering".</ref>
<ref>Reinhard Oehme [https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.100.1503 , Phys. Rev. 100, 1503 - 1512 (1955)]“Dispersion Relations for Pion-Nucleon Scattering” I.</ref>
There is good agreement with the experimental results of the Fermi Group
at Chicago, the [[Lindenbaum]] Group at Brookhaven and others.
The GMO sum rule is often used in the analysis of the pion-nucleon system.
<ref>For Example: V. V. Abaev, P. Metsä and M. E. Sainio
[https://doi.org/10.1140%2Fepja%2Fi2007-10377-6 , Eur. Phys. J. A 32, 321 (2007)]
 “The Goldberger-Miyazawa-Oehme sum rule revisited”.arXiv:0704.3167v2 [hep-ph]</ref>
Oehme published a proper derivation of hadronic forward dispersion relations on the basis of
local quantum field theory in an article published in [[Nuovo Cimento|''Il Nuovo Cimento'']].<ref>Reinhard Oehme [https://doi.org/10.1007%2FBF02746363 , Il Nuovo Cimento 4(1956)1316] “Causality and Dispersion Relations for the Scattering of Mesons by fixed Nucleons”; Appendix: Proof of Relativistic Forward Dispersion Relations.</ref> His proof remains
valid in [[gauge theories]] with [[Color confinement|confinement]].<ref>Reinhard Oehme, Talk given at 11th International Conference on Mathematical Physics, Paris, France, 18-23 Jul 1994  {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805150929/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?eprint=hep-th/9412040|title=, Int. J. Mod. Phys. A10:1995-2014,1995.}} “Analytic structure of amplitudes in gauge theories with confinement”.</ref>
The analytic connection Oehme found between particle and antiparticle amplitudes is the first example of a fundamental feature of local quantum field theory: the [[Crossing (physics)|crossing]] property. It is proven here, in a non-perturbative setting, on the basis of the analytic properties of amplitudes which are a consequence of locality and spectrum, like the dispersion relations. For generalizations, one still relies mostly on [[perturbation theory]].
For the purpose of using the powerful methods of the theory of functions
of several complex variables for the proof of non-forward dispersion relations,
and for [[Analytic function|analytic]] properties of other [[Green's function]]s, Oehme formulated and proved a fundamental theorem which he called the [[edge-of-the-wedge theorem]] (Keilkanten Theorem). This work was done mainly in the fall of 1956 at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in collaboration with [[Hans-Joachim Bremermann]] and [[John G. Taylor]].
<ref>H. J. Bremermann, R. Oehme and J.G. Taylor,
“UNE DEMONSTRATION POSSIBLE DES RELATIONS DE DISPERSION”
presented at Les Problemes Mathematiques de la Theorie Quantique des Champs,
Colloques Internationaux du CNRS, Lille, France, 3-8 Juin 1957, printed in
Colloques Internationaux du Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique,
LXXV, 169 (1959).</ref><ref>H.J. Bremermann, R. Oehme and J.G. Taylor
[https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.109.2178 , Phys.Rev.109(1958) 2178]
“Proof of Dispersion Relations in Quantized Field Theories”;
Appendix: “The Edge of the Wedge Theorem”. (This paper contains
references to the work of [[Nikolay Bogoliubov]] and others.)</ref>
Using microscopic causality and spectral properties, the Bremermann–Oehme–Taylor (BOT) theorem provides
an initial region of analyticity, which can be enlarged by analytic completion.
Oehme first presented these results at the Princeton University Colloquium
during the winter semester 1956/57. Independently, a different and elaborate proof of
non-forward dispersion relations has been published by [[Nikolay Bogoliubov]] and collaborators.
<ref>N. N. Bogoliubov and D. V. Shirkov, "Introduction to the Theory of Quantized Fields",
John Wiley & Sons, Incorporated 1959, {{ISBN|0-471-04223-4}} / 9780471042235.</ref>
The edge-of-the-wedge theorem by BOT has many other applications.
For example, it can be used to show that, in the presence of (spontaneous) violations of [[Lorentz invariance]], micro-causality (locality), together
with positivity of the energy, implies [[Lorentz invariance]]  of the energy-
momentum spectrum.<ref>H.J. Borchers (Dec 1984)  "Locality and Covariance of the Spectrum", Fizika 17:289-304, 1985 and references given there.</ref>
Together with [[Marvin L. Goldberger]] and [[Yoichiro Nambu]], Oehme also has formulated dispersion relations
for nucleon-nucleon scattering.<ref>Marvin L. Goldberger, Yoichiro Nambu and Reinhard Oehme,[http://adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1957AnPhy...2..226G , Ann.Phys.(N.Y.) 2:226(1957)] "Dispersion Relations for Nucleon-Nucleon Scattering." In accordance with the results of Oehme about the analytic continuation of amplitudes, these relations contain
integrals involving nucleon-nucleon and nucleon-antinucleon total cross sections, as well as
absolute squares of annihilation amplitudes.</ref>

===Charge conjugation non-conservation===

On August 7, 1956, Oehme wrote a letter <ref>Yang, C.N. (1983).
''Selected papers 1945-1980, with commentary (Chen Ning Yang)'', p.32, 33.
W.H. Freeman, San Francisco 1983. {{ISBN|0-7167-1406-X}}.</ref> to [[C.N. Yang]] in which it is
shown that [[weak interactions]] must violate [[charge conjugation]] conservation in the event
of a positive outcome of the polarization experiment in [[beta-decay]]. Since [[parity (physics)|parity]]
conservation leads to the same restrictions, he points out that C and P must BOTH
be violated in order to get an asymmetry. Hence, at the level of ordinary weak
interactions, CP is the relevant symmetry, and not C and P individually.
<ref>Coulomb distortions of the electron wave function can be experimentally
separated due to their Z and p dependence.</ref> Violation of C is one of the fundamental conditions <ref>[[Andrei Sakharov]],
Pisma Zh. Eksp. Teor. Fiz. 5 (1967), 32</ref> for the matter-antimatter
asymmetry of the  Universe.
The results of Oehme form the basis for the
later experimental  effort to study [[CP Symmetry]], and the fundamental discovery of  non-conservation at a lower level of interaction strength.
<ref>J.H. Christensen, J. Cronin, V.F. Fitch, and R. Turlay
[https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.13.138  Phys. Rev. Lett. 13, 138 - 140 (1964)]
“Evidence for the 2π Decay of the K20 Meson”.</ref><ref>[[James W. Cronin]]
[https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.53.373  Rev. Mod. Phys. 53, 373 - 383 (1981)]
“CP symmetry violation—the search for its origin”, Nobel lecture, Dec 1980.</ref>
As indicated above, the letter is reprinted
in the book on Selected Papers by [[C.N. Yang]].<ref>Yang, C.N. (1983).
''Selected papers 1945-1980, with commentary (Chen Ning Yang)'', p.32, 33.
W.H. Freeman, San Francisco 1983. {{ISBN|0-7167-1406-X}}</ref>
Prompted by the letter, [[Tsung-Dao Lee|T.D. Lee]], R Oehme and C.N. Yang provided a detailed discussion of
the interplay of non-invariance under P, C and T, and of applications to
the [[kaon]] - anti-kaon complex.<ref>T.D. Lee (Columbia U.), Reinhard Oehme, Chen-Ning Yang (Princeton, Inst. Advanced Study) {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805225625/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHRVA,106,340|title=,  Phys.Rev.106:340-345,1957.}} “Remarks on Possible Noninvariance Under Time Reversal and Charge Conjugation.”</ref> Their results are of importance for the description of the [[CP violation]] discovered later. In their paper the authors already consider non-invariance under T ([[T-symmetry|time reversal]])
and hence, given the assumption of [[CPT symmetry]], also under CP.

===Propagators and OZ superconvergence relations===

In connection with an exact structure analysis for [[gauge theory]] [[propagator]]s,
undertaken by Oehme in collaboration with [[Wolfhart Zimmermann]],
<ref>Reinhard Oehme, Wolfhart Zimmermann (Chicago U., EFI & Chicago U. & Munich, Max Planck Inst.)  EFI-79/28-CHICAGO, May 1979, 47pp.
{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121211153218/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHRVA,D21,471|title=, Phys.Rev.D21:471,1980}} "Quark And Gluon Propagators In Quantum Chromodynamics".</ref>
<ref>Reinhard Oehme, Wolfhart Zimmermann,  EFI-79/51-CHICAGO, MPI-PAE/PTh 38/79, (Received Oct (1979){{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805173841/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHRVA,D21,1661|title=, Phys.Rev.D21:1661, 1980.}} "Gauge Field Propagator and the Number Of Fermion Fields".</ref> he obtained [[superconvergence]] relations for theories where the number of [[matter]] fields (flavors) is below a given limit. These Oehme–Zimmernann relations provide a link between long- and short-distance properties of the theory. They are of importance for [[gluon]] [[color confinement|confinement]].<ref>Reinhard Oehme, MPI-PAE-PTH-39-90, EFI-90-50, Jul 1990. 34pp.
{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805133420/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHRVA,D42,4209|title=,  Phys.Rev.D42:4209-4221,1990.}} "Renormalization group, BRST cohomology, and the problem of confinement". (This paper contains references to the work of K. Nishijima and others.)</ref>
These results about propagators depend essentially only upon general principles.

===Reduction of quantum field theories===

As a general method of imposing restrictions on quantum field theories with
several parameters, Oehme and Zimmermann have introduced a theory of reduction
of [[coupling constants]].<ref>Reinhard Oehme, Wolfhart Zimmermann,  MPI-PAE/PTh 60/82, {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120806004109/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=CMPHA,97,569|title=, Commun.Math.Phys.97:569,1985}} "Relation Between Effective Couplings for Asymptotically Free Models".</ref>
<ref>Reinhard Oehme, Klaus Sibold, Wolfhart Zimmermann,  MPI-PAE/PTh 36/84, May 1984 {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805130326/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHLTA,B147,115|title=, Phys.Lett.B147:115,1984.}} "Renormalization Group Equations With Vanishing Lowest Order Of The Primary Beta Function". MPI-PAE/PTh 87/84, EFI-85-05-CHICAGO, Dec 1984. 11pp. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120806000543/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PHLTA,B153,142|title=, Phys.Lett.B153:142,1985.}} "Construction Of Gauge Theories With A Single Coupling Parameter For Yang-Mills And Matter Fields".</ref>
This method is based upon the [[renormalization group]], and is more general than the
imposition of [[symmetries]].<ref name=OE>R. Oehme (CERN) . CERN-TH-4245/85, Aug 1985. 34pp. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20121211175258/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=PTPSA,86,215|title=, Prog.Theor.Phys.Suppl.86:215,1986}} "Reduction And Reparametrization Of Quantum Field Theories". (Dedicated to Yoichiro Nambu on the occasion of his 65th birthday.) This paper contains further references</ref><ref>W. Zimmermann, MPI-PAE/PTh-49/84, Jul 1984. 24pp. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120805220708/http://www.slac.stanford.edu/spires/find/hep/www?j=CMPHA,97,211|title=, Commun.Math.Phys.97:211,1985.}} "Reduction in the Number of Coupling Parameters". (Dedicated to the memory of Kurt Symanzik.)</ref>
There are solutions of the reduction equations which do not correspond to additional symmetries, but may be related to other characteristic aspects of the theory. On the other hand, supersymmetric theories do come out as possible solutions. This is an important example for the appearance of [[supersymmetry]] without imposing it explicitly. The reduction theory is finding many applications,<ref name=OE/> theoretical<ref>For example:
Reinhard Oehme, Talk given at Ringberg Symposium on Quantum Field Theory, Ringberg Castle, Germany, 21-24 Jun 1998.
Lect. Notes in Phys.558:136-156, 2000 “Reduction of coupling parameters and duality.”</ref>
and phenomenological.
<ref>For example: J. Kubo, M. Mondragon, G. Zoupanos, hep-ph/9703289, Acta Phys. Polon.B27:3911-3944, 1997 "Unification beyond GUTs: Gauge Yukawa unification", Lectures given at Cracow School of Theoretical Physics, 1996 and  Bruno Pontecorvo School on Elementary Particle Physics, 1996.</ref>

===Other contributions===

Further contributions by Oehme, like those involving complex [[angular momentum]],
<ref>For example: Reinhard Oehme, “High Energy Scattering and Relativistic Dispersion Theory”,  Ravenna Lectures, in ’’Dispersion Relations and their Connection with Causality’’, edited by [[E. P. Wigner]] (Academic Press, New York 1964) pp. 167-256.</ref> Rising cross sections,<ref>Reinhard Oehme, “Rising Cross Sections”, Lecture given in July 1971 at DESY, before rising cross sections were experimentally discovered. Springer Tracts in Modern Physics 61:109 (1972).</ref> broken symmetries, [[current algebra]]s and weak interactions,<ref>For example: Reinhard Oehme [https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.16.215 , Phys.Rev.Lett. 16, 215-217 (1966).] "Current Algebras and the Suppression of Leptonic Meson Decays with DeltaS=1".</ref> as well as chapters in books.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A FEW PUBLICATIONS WITH COMMENTS |url=http://home.uchicago.edu/~roehme/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303230459/http://home.uchicago.edu/~roehme/ |archive-date=2016-03-03 |access-date=2025-10-21 |website=home.uchicago.edu}}</ref>
